newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia Serb army chief Mladic succssor takes oath.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia Serb army chief Mladic succssor takes oath.

text.p: Major General Pero Colic, named to succeed indicted war criminal Ratko Mladic as Bosnian Serb military chief, formally took office on Sunday, the official news agency SRNA reported.

At a swearing-in ceremony attended by Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic, he vowed to "defend the sovereignty, territory, independence and constitution of the fatherland, and loyally serve the interests of its people".
The ceremony in Pale, the Serbs' political headquarters east of Sarajevo, marked the latest stage in Plavsic's "restructuring" of the army's command.
She announced on Saturday that she had retired Mladic and his deputy as part of an extensive shakeup.
Mladic and his senior officers met later in their headquarters at Han Pijesak to discuss the dismissals.
It was not immediately clear how they would react to Sunday's ceremony, although more than 24 hours after the dismissals were announced, there was no sign that any army action was imminent.
Western mediators and NATO officials said it may take some days to determine whether the sacked officers would accept Plavsic's decree or fight to retain their jobs.
After the swearing-in ceremony, Colic told SRNA he had not expected to be offered the most senior job in the Bosnian Serb army.

"I was surprised at the invitation for me to accept one of the duties bearing the most responsibility at a moment characterised by a very difficult military and political situation, but my conscience motivated me to accept and help the Serb people to once and for all create the Republika Srpska (Bosnian Serb Republic)," SRNA quoted Colic as saying.
He said the new general staff was made up of soldiers well tested in war who "will operate in keeping with orders from the Supreme Command, as demanded by military-political circumstances".
Plavsic is heads the Supreme Command, which is a political rather than military body.

Colic's cooperative remarks contrast with a long-running feud between the former military command led by Mladic, and the Bosnian Serb political leadership which errupted into a public row over recent weeks.
Figures like international High Representative Carl Bildt have long been demanding that Mladic be extradited to a tribunal in The Hague to answer charges of war crimes and genocide.
He stands accused of directing the siege of Sarajevo and overseeing the massacre of some 8,000 unarmed Moslems from the enclave of Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia last year.
